explanation: Fires most strongly on ' with' in the GPL licence boilerplate 'You should have received a copy ... along with', and on 'not' in 'if not, write to the'. More weakly it fires on predictable function words or adverbs that finish a stock phrase ('By using this website', 'this works', 'is part of', 'still active'). Elsewhere it is weak and scattered.

Fires on library, package or class-name pieces in code and tech talk: import path segments ('/testify', '/pkg', '/jquery'), framework names (redis, Redis) and CamelCase API subwords ('Manager' in CLLocationManager or ApplicationManager). Strongest inside import or script-src paths. Plain prose barely fires it.

Fires on the verb 'date(s)/dating' in 'X dates back to / dates from [a time]', the phrase that gives the historical origin of something. Weaker on other origin and age phrasing ('genesis', 'going back to', 'since 1971', 'as far back as').

Fires on tokens near the start of a document or section, such as the first word or subword of an abstract or introduction ('Noisy', 'Exposure', 'Serum'), the year slot after a date in 'On 30 August 2010', 'Category:' and ISBN digits. It seems to track position at a document or section opening rather than any token identity.

Fires on word-internal pieces, often the first subword, when a word is split into several tokens. This is mostly in non-English text (German, Portuguese, French, Romanian) and in rare or split English words ('pan|icking', 'f|oment', 'herm|aph'). The concept is the tokenization fragment, not its meaning.

Fires on the second subword piece of proper names and technical words that tokenize into fragments, especially 'Mal', 'Mar', 'Vo' (Voivodeship), 'gl' (hemagglutinin) and 'ag'. These are mostly Romance or Slavic place and person names plus chemical or biological terms. Ordinary words do not fire it.

Fires on the tag-name token right after '<' in HTML or XML markup ('<a', '<option', '<li', '<span', '<label', '<string', '<h3'). It is strongest for '<a' links inside nested lists or menus. Weaker on the first attribute name or quote inside a tag ('value', 'type').

A diffuse mixture with no clear shared feature: 'key' in SSH or openssl contexts, 'new' before a product or project, condition or medical nouns (autism, cataracts), and assorted content nouns and verbs ('expansion', 'tested', 'learned').

Fires on the number two in any form: '2', 'two', 'iki', 'both', 'dual', and also 'bi-' as a prefix. It is strongest when the number is a count before a noun ('two groups', '2 bathrooms', 'Top 2'). Weaker for ordinal or other uses ('second', '2-1').

Fires on function words and possessives inside evaluative or emphatic phrasing: the possessive 's/'s ('New York's', 'aviation's'), 'what better', 'actually', 'even', 'most' and 'more likely'. Generic or neutral function-word contexts get only weak activation.

Fires on the last subword piece that completes a multi-token name or identifier: a digit or letter ending an alphanumeric code ('p5|3', 'B1|2', 'F-3|5', 'H-1|B', 'Android 5.|1') or the end of a split proper noun or word ('Gilm|our', 'wholegr|ain', 'Vernon'). Whole common words barely fire it.

Fires on subword pieces inside technical, mostly biomedical or scientific terms ('antigen', 'interleuk|in', 'interfer|on', 'somatost|atin', 'tuberc|ulin', '-yl' chemical suffixes, anatomy terms). The text is usually an academic abstract. Weak on everyday vocabulary.

Has no clear concept. It fires on a scattered mix: GPL boilerplate ('2 along', 'version 3 of'), word-ending suffixes in technical terms ('-ic', '-ase', '-ings'), commas in names or dates and math operators.

Fires on the number or name of a part in a sequence of installments: 'Episode 18', 'Part 19', 'Season/series 4', 'Experiment 1', 'Division One', 'Act 1', 'first period'. It fires on the ordinal or number token that follows such a section label, or on the label after an ordinal. Weaker on list markers and other enumerations.

Fires inside templated algebra word problems ('Let p be h(0)', 'Let j be 2/(-1)', 'Suppose -3*n ...'). It fires on 'be' after 'Let x', on '/(-' division with a negative and on minus signs or operators that follow 'Suppose'. Text that is not in that math-problem format gets close to nothing.

Fires on the first subword piece of a word split into several tokens, often a capital or consonant-cluster opening ('Fr|ondaie', 'de|bridement', 'Br|ötzmann', 'C|RYING', 'dr|ifter'). It covers names, foreign words and technical terms. The trigger is the opening of a multi-token word.

Fires on stems and morpheme pieces inside non-English European words, especially compound or derived words in German, Scandinavian, Hungarian, Finnish and Romance languages ('Wall|on|ie', 'naturl|igt|vis', 'af|ghan|ischen'). It is driven by being mid-word in foreign-language text.

A mixture: name pieces inside CamelCase or multi-token identifiers ('Coin|Desk', 'Vr|Math', 'linux/kernel'), word endings in Danish or Finnish text, and English verbs like 'make' after 'to'. There is no single shared concept.

Fires on leading tab-indentation tokens at the start of a line of code, or on tab separators inside tab-aligned text, especially multiple tabs in Go, C, Lua or JS. Weaker on ';\n' or '{\n' line endings and on space indentation.

Fires on boilerplate or structural tokens in web-page and metadata text: newlines after email header or date fields, 'Shares', 'Share this post', 'Posted:', 'Released', share-URL parts and config keywords ('compile', 'shortcut'). Some technical compound nouns also fire it ('Rankine Cycle', 'cell walls'). Overall a loose mixture.

A broad, unfocused mixture. The most regular pattern is the space token before a year or number after 'from X to', 'in' or 'than' ('to 1747', 'in 1629', 'larger than 64kb'). It also fires on assorted code tokens and adjectives ('good', 'greatly').
